catalog_quote: ... accent in Chuvash is phonologically irrelevant, since its placement or misplacement does not create a different word . Al- though the accent does not occur on any fixed syllable as in some languages, it is as far towards the end of the word as the following rules allow . These formulations apply to the literary language, or Formal Written Chuvash; in the dialects, there may be different practices . 1.31 The accent is on the last syllable unless this contains the reduced vowel phonemes / ě / or / ǎ / . / lašá / / ěné / / kamaká / / sarlaká / horse cow stove widely 1.32 If the last syllable does contain / e / or / ǎ /, then the accent is on the syllable immediately preceding . Should the last two syllables both contain / e / or / ǎ /, then the accent will im- mediately precede those two syllables . / álăk / / yěnérčěk / / ěślérěměr / / kálăttămăr / door saddle we worked we woul…
sweep_summary: Chuvash (chuv1255, catalog classification weight, deciding source Krueger 1961 snippet view, corroborated by Dobrovolsky 1999). it is library print only and rated medium priority (theoretical, likely Krueger-based). Instead this search of works with stress in the title obtained the open text of Dobrovolsky 1999 (ICPhS-14, IPA proceedings site), with updated: a first-hand instrumental study confirming stress on the last full vowel (weight-sensitive, unbounded) and refining the default clause (all-reduced words are phonetically stressless; the perceived initial stress is an early F0 fall; a South Chuvashia dialect has a right-edge default). It confirms the catalog's weight coding and does not supersede Krueger 1961 as the source of the full rule. Krueger 1961 full text remains unobtained (HathiTrust 403, archive.org lending-only). The SPA 1979 entry already held by the project (Andreev 1966: 46 quoted) also confirms.

new_statements.reading: First-hand phonetic study on the author's own 1994 field recordings (standard dialect, 4 speakers, disyllabic citation forms). Word stress is assigned to the last full (non-reduced) vowel of the word - a weight-sensitive, unbounded right-edge rule, exactly the catalog's 'weight' coding with full-vs-reduced-vowel weight. The refinement: words containing only reduced vowels carry no phonetic stress; the reported initial 'default' stress is an early intonational F0 fall, so the 'else initial' clause is an intonation fact, not a stress-assignment fact (the catalog's default_when_no_heavy field already records this). He also notes a South Chuvashia dialect where the default is right-edge, and a layer of rhythmic stresses not analysed. Standard-dialect stress on the last full vowel is confirmed with statistics (duration ratio, total amplitude ratio).

sources.note: First-hand instrumental study (author's own 1994 recordings in the Chuvash Republic, 4 speakers, disyllabic citation forms; Kay CSL, ANOVA/Scheffe/t-tests). Vowels are 'full' /i y e ö u a/ vs 'reduced' /ĕ ă/. Stress falls on the last full vowel of the word (confirmed phonetically by duration and total-amplitude ratios for FF/FR/RF words). Words with only reduced vowels (RR) show no significant stress correlates; the perceived 'default' initial stress is an early F0 fall of the citation-form intonation (Table 5: 70.6% of RR tokens fall on V1). He notes (p. 539) one speaker from South Chuvashia…

sources.quote: "In the absence of reduced vowels stress almost always falls on the final syllable.... In words with reduced vowels stress falls on the last full vowel.... If all the vowels in a word are reduced, stress falls on the first syllable. Russian loanwords preserve the Russian stress in the base form, but in all other forms they follow the Chuvash stress patterns." (Andreev 1966, p.46) "Stress...is not the strong emphasis found in English words, but simply a slightly increased intensity of sound, perhaps accompanied with a slight shift of pitch. The stress on all syllables is approximately the same.

tone.quote: In Balkar I found a group of unstressed words pronounced on the very low breath effort ... An expiratory accent is impossible in such words. Accentual innovations of a similar type take place in Chuvash. They are conditioned by the arise of “reduced” vowels. These vowels resulted from the phonologization of a prosody whose phonetic nature retains unclear. My work with Chuvash speakers revealed a low level of breath activity. .Such “soft” vowels can not function as an anchor for phrase accent which is equivalent to stress in Turkic languages. If a word contains just “reduced” vowels, it receives just a slight prominence on the first syllable. Otherwise, the last full vowel is stressed (cf. [2]).

tone.quote: The language of the Volga Bulghars is limitedly attested in epitaph inscriptions in the Arabic script dating from the 13th–14th centuries (Erdal 1993). These records clearly indicate Volga Bulghar as a Chuvash-type Turkic language [...] || 27.3.5 Suprasegmentals: The accent system represented in standard Chuvash is close to that of the Viryal dialect. As a general rule, the last syllable with a full vowel is stressed: aván ‘good’, sə̂orá ‘beer’, karlánkə̂ ‘throat’. In the words with reduced vowels only, the accent falls on the first syllable: xə́rlə ‘red’, və̂́orə̂om ‘long’. Most of Anatri varieties represent a more innovative system where the last syllable is usually stressed, regardless of the quality of the vowel
